title: 23.0 Basics
text:
Throughout this chapter:

Let \(k\) be a fixed base field.
A \(k\)-variety is defined as a geometrically reduced, separated scheme of finite type over \(k\).
We denote by \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\) the category of schemes of finite type over \(k\), and by \(\mathrm{Var}/k\) the full subcategory of \(k\)-varieties.
For an affine scheme \(X = \operatorname{Spec} A\), \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra.



Definition 1 (Algebraic Group and Abelian Variety)  

An algebraic group over \(k\) is a group object in the category \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\). That is, it is a scheme \(G\) of finite type over \(k\) equipped with \(k\)-morphisms:

Multiplication: \(m: G \times_k G \to G\),
Inverse: \(i: G \to G\),
Identity section: \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\),

satisfying the usual group axioms.
An abelian variety is an algebraic variety \(A \in \mathrm{Var}/k\) which is a proper, geometrically connected group object in \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\).



Lemma 1 (Smoothness of Geometrically Reduced Groups) Any geometrically reduced algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\) is smooth. Consequently, its connected components coincide with its irreducible components.


Proof. Proof sketch. Since \(G_{\bar{k}}\) is reduced and of finite type over an algebraically closed field, its smooth locus \(\operatorname{Sm}(G_{\bar{k}})\) is open and non-empty. For any closed point \(g \in G(\bar{k})\), the group translation \(L_g: G_{\bar{k}} \to G_{\bar{k}}\) is an automorphism mapping smooth points to smooth points. Transitivity of translations implies that every point of \(G_{\bar{k}}\) is smooth. Thus \(G\) is smooth over \(k\). Because smooth schemes are locally irreducible, the connected components must coincide with the irreducible components.


Lemma 2 (Rigidity Lemma) Let \(X, Y, Z\) be varieties over \(k\) with \(X\) proper and geometrically irreducible, and \(Y\) geometrically irreducible. Let \[
f: X \times_k Y \to Z
\] be a \(k\)-morphism. Suppose there exists a \(k\)-rational point \(y_0 \in Y(k)\) such that \(f(X \times \{y_0\}) = \{z_0\}\) for some \(z_0 \in Z(k)\).
Then \(f\) factors through the canonical projection \(p_2: X \times_k Y \to Y\). That is, there exists a morphism \(g: Y \to Z\) such that \(f = g \circ p_2\).


Proof. Fix a rational point \(x_0 \in X(k)\) (extending scalars to \(\bar{k}\) if necessary). Define \(g: Y \to Z\) by the composition: \[
Y \xrightarrow{x_0 \times \mathrm{id}_Y} X \times_k Y \xrightarrow{f} Z.
\] We show that \(f(x, y) = g(y)\) for all \(x \in X, y \in Y\).

Choose an affine open neighborhood \(U \subseteq Z\) containing \(z_0\). The complement \(Z \setminus U\) is closed in \(Z\), so \(f^{-1}(Z \setminus U)\) is closed in \(X \times_k Y\).
Since \(X\) is proper over \(k\), the projection \(p_2: X \times_k Y \to Y\) is universally closed. Thus: \[
W := p_2\big(f^{-1}(Z \setminus U)\big) = \{ y \in Y \mid \exists x \in X \text{ with } f(x, y) \notin U \}
\] is a closed subset of \(Y\).
By hypothesis, \(f(X \times \{y_0\}) = \{z_0\} \subseteq U\), so \(y_0 \notin W\). Hence \(Y \setminus W\) is an open neighborhood of \(y_0\). Pick an affine open neighborhood \(V \subseteq Y \setminus W\) containing \(y_0\).
By construction, \(f(X \times V) \subseteq U\). Since \(U\) is affine, we may choose a closed embedding \(U \hookrightarrow \mathbb{A}^n\). For every closed point \(y \in V\), the fiber \(X \times \{y\} \cong X\) is proper and connected. Its image in the affine space \(\mathbb{A}^n\) under \(f\) must be both proper and affine, hence it must be a single point: \[
f(X \times \{y\}) = \{f(x_0, y)\} = \{g(y)\}.
\]
Therefore, \(f|_{X \times V} = (g \circ p_2)|_{X \times V}\). Because \(X \times_k Y\) is reduced and \(Z\) is separated, two morphisms agreeing on a non-empty open subscheme are identical everywhere (Reduced-to-Separated Theorem). Thus \(f = g \circ p_2\).



Proposition 1 (Proper Connected Groups are Abelian) Any proper connected smooth algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\) is abelian. In particular, abelian varieties are commutative.


Proof. Consider the commutator morphism: \[
f: G \times_k G \to G, \quad (x, y) \mapsto x y x^{-1} y^{-1}.
\] Observe that \(f(G \times \{e\}) = \{e\}\). Since \(G\) is proper and connected, Lemma 2 implies that \(f\) factors through the projection to the second factor: \[
f(x, y) = f(e, y) = e y e^{-1} y^{-1} = e.
\] Hence \(xyx^{-1}y^{-1} = e\) for all \(x, y \in G\), meaning \(xy = yx\). Thus \(G\) is abelian.



Proposition 2 (Separatedness of Group Schemes) Every group scheme \(G\) of finite type over a field \(k\) is separated.


Proof. A morphism \(G \to \operatorname{Spec} k\) is separated if and only if the diagonal \(\Delta: G \to G \times_k G\) is a closed immersion.
Consider the difference morphism \(\mu: G \times_k G \to G\) defined by \((g_1, g_2) \mapsto g_1 g_2^{-1}\). The diagonal \(\Delta(G)\) is the scheme-theoretic pullback of the identity section \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\) along \(\mu\): \[
\begin{CD}
G @>{\Delta}>> G \times_k G \\
@VVV @VV{\mu}V \\
\operatorname{Spec} k @>{e}>> G
\end{CD}
\] Because base change preserves closed immersions, it suffices to prove that \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\) is a closed immersion. The image of \(e\) is a single point \(e \in G\). Since \(G\) is of finite type over \(k\), the point \(e\) has residue field \(k(e) \cong k\) and is closed. Thus \(e\) is a closed immersion, which implies \(\Delta\) is a closed immersion. Therefore, \(G\) is separated over \(k\).


Lemma 3 (Open Subgroups are Closed)  

If \(G\) is a group scheme over \(k\) such that \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \times_k G_{\mathrm{red}}\) is reduced, then \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \hookrightarrow G\) is a closed subgroup scheme. In particular, if \(G_{\mathrm{red}}\) is geometrically reduced (e.g., if \(k\) is perfect), then \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \hookrightarrow G\) is a smooth closed subgroup scheme of \(G\).
Let \(\varphi: G' \to G\) be a homomorphism of group schemes over \(k\). If the image \(\varphi(G')\) is open in \(G\), then \(\varphi(G')\) is also closed in \(G\).



Proof. Proof of (2). Let \(U = \varphi(G') \subseteq G\) be open. Endow the complement \(Z := G \setminus U\) with the reduced subscheme structure. It suffices to show that \(Z\) is open.
Consider the action map \(Z \times_k G' \to G\) given by \((z, g') \mapsto z \cdot \varphi(g')\). For any \(g' \in G'\), the translation \(x \mapsto x \cdot \varphi(g')\) is an automorphism of \(G\). Since \(U = \varphi(G')\) is stable under right multiplication by \(\varphi(G')\), its complement \(Z\) is also stable under multiplication by \(\varphi(G')\).
Because translations are open morphisms, the image of \(Z \times_k G' \to G\) is a union of translates of \(Z\), which is open. But this image is precisely \(Z\) itself. Hence \(Z\) is open, which proves \(U = G \setminus Z\) is closed.


Lemma 4 (Immersions of Group Schemes are Closed) Let \(i: G' \hookrightarrow G\) be an immersion of group schemes over \(k\). Then \(i\) is a closed immersion.


Proof. Without loss of generality, assume \(G\) and \(G'\) are reduced. Let \(\overline{G'}\) denote the scheme-theoretic closure of \(i(G')\) in \(G\) equipped with the reduced structure. Since multiplication \(m: G \times_k G \to G\) is continuous and maps \(G' \times_k G'\) into \(G'\), it maps the closure \(\overline{G'} \times_k \overline{G'}\) into \(\overline{G'}\). Thus \(\overline{G'}\) is a closed subgroup scheme of \(G\).
Since \(i\) is an immersion, \(i(G')\) is an open subscheme of \(\overline{G'}\). By Lemma 3, an open subgroup scheme of \(\overline{G'}\) is closed in \(\overline{G'}\). Hence \(i(G') = \overline{G'}\), so \(i(G')\) is closed in \(G\).


Lemma 5 (Connected Implies Irreducible) Let \(G\) be a group scheme of finite type over \(k\).

If \(G\) is irreducible, then \(G\) is quasi-compact.
If \(G\) is connected, then \(G\) is irreducible.


(Reference: The Stacks Project, Tag 047R, Tag 047S).


Proposition 3 (Subgroup Schemes and Kernels)  

A closed subscheme \(H \subseteq G\) is a normal subgroup scheme (denoted \(H \trianglelefteq G\)) if for all \(T \in \mathrm{Sch}/k\), \(H(T)\) is a normal subgroup of \(G(T)\) (equivalently, \(H(R) \trianglelefteq G(R)\) for all \(R \in \mathrm{Alg}_k\)).
Let \(\varphi: G \to G'\) be a homomorphism of group schemes. The scheme-theoretic kernel is defined as the fiber product: \[
\ker \varphi := \operatorname{Spec} k \times_{e, G', \varphi} G = \varphi^{-1}(e).
\] Then \(\ker \varphi\) is a closed normal subgroup scheme of \(G\).
On functor of points, \(\ker(\varphi)(R) = \ker(G(R) \to G'(R))\) for all \(R \in \mathrm{Alg}_k\).



Proposition 4 (Homomorphisms and Dimensions) Let \(\varphi: G \to G'\) be a homomorphism of algebraic groups over \(k\).

The scheme-theoretic image \(\varphi(G)\) is closed in \(G'\). We denote \(\operatorname{Im} \varphi := \varphi(G)_{\mathrm{red}}\).
Dimension Formula: \[
\dim G = \dim \ker \varphi + \dim \operatorname{Im} \varphi.
\]



Proof. Idea of Proof. By Chevalley’s Theorem on constructible sets, \(\varphi(G)\) contains a dense open subset of its closure. Group translations then show that \(\varphi(G)\) is open in its closure \(\overline{\varphi(G)}\). By Lemma 3, an open subgroup of \(\overline{\varphi(G)}\) is closed, whence \(\varphi(G) = \overline{\varphi(G)}\).


Proposition 5 (Image Factorization and Flatness)  

If \(G'\) is reduced and \(\varphi: G \to G'\) is dominant, then \(\varphi\) is an fppf morphism (faithfully flat locally of finite presentation).
If \(G\) is smooth, any homomorphism \(\varphi: G \to H\) factors canonically as: \[
G \xrightarrow{p} I \xrightarrow{i} H
\] where \(p\) is fppf and \(i\) is a closed immersion into \(H\).



Proof. Set \(I := \varphi(G)\) with reduced subscheme structure. By generic flatness, there exists a dense open subscheme \(U \subseteq I\) over which \(\varphi^{-1}(U) \to U\) is flat. Since translations by rational points (over \(\bar{k}\)) act transitively on \(I\), translates of \(U\) cover \(I\). Therefore, \(\varphi_{\bar{k}}\) is flat everywhere. Being surjective (image is closed) between noetherian schemes, it is fppf.



Remark 1 (Hopf Algebras and Functor of Points). An affine scheme \(G = \operatorname{Spec} A\) is a group scheme if and only if its coordinate ring \(A = \mathcal{O}(G)\) is a commutative Hopf algebra over \(k\), equipped with:

Comultiplication \(\Delta: A \to A \otimes_k A\),
Counit \(\varepsilon: A \to k\),
Antipode \(S: A \to A\).

We have an anti-equivalence of categories: \[
\{\text{Commutative f.g. Hopf } k\text{-algebras}\}^{\mathrm{op}} \xrightarrow{\sim} \{\text{Affine / Linear } k\text{-algebraic groups}\}.
\]
Via the functor of points, the Yoneda embedding yields a fully faithful functor: \[
\mathbf{GrpSch}/k \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Alg}_k, \mathbf{Grp}), \quad G \mapsto (R \mapsto G(R) = \operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(A, R)).
\]


Example 1 (Basic Examples)  

Finite Constant Group: Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite abstract group. The coordinate algebra is \(A = \prod_{g \in \Gamma} k \cdot e_g\) with orthogonal idempotents \(e_g\).

Comultiplication: \(\Delta(e_x) = \sum_{yz = x} e_y \otimes e_z\),
Antipode: \(S(e_x) = e_{x^{-1}}\),
Counit: \(\varepsilon(e_x) = \delta_{x, e}\).

On \(R\)-points: \[
G(R) = \left\{ (r_g)_{g \in \Gamma} \in R^\Gamma \;\middle|\; \sum_{g \in \Gamma} r_g = 1, \, r_g r_h = 0 \text{ for } g \neq h \right\}.
\]
Standard Matrix Groups (for \(n \in \mathbb{N}\)):

General Linear Group \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) (Reductive): \[
\mathrm{GL}_n(R) = \{ M \in \mathrm{Mat}_{n \times n}(R) \mid \det(M) \in R^\times \}.
\]
Standard Borel Subgroup \(B_n\) (Solvable): \[
B_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R) \mid x_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i > j \}.
\]
Standard Unipotent Subgroup \(U_n\) (Unipotent): \[
U_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in B_n(R) \mid x_{ii} = 1 \text{ for all } 1 \le i \le n \}.
\]
Standard Maximal Torus \(T_n\) (Split Torus): \[
T_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in B_n(R) \mid x_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i \neq j \} \cong (\mathbb{G}_{m, R})^n.
\]

These satisfy the inclusion hierarchy: \[
U_n \trianglelefteq B_n \subseteq \mathrm{GL}_n, \quad T_n \subseteq B_n, \quad B_n = T_n \ltimes U_n.
\]




Proposition 6 (Existence of the Largest Étale Subalgebra) Let \(X\) be a scheme of finite type over \(k\). Then there exists a unique largest étale \(k\)-subalgebra \(\pi_0(X) \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\).


Proof. 

If \(A_1, A_2 \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\) are étale \(k\)-subalgebras, the subring generated by them is the image of the canonical map \(A_1 \otimes_k A_2 \to \mathcal{O}(X)\). Since the tensor product of étale algebras is étale and any quotient of an étale algebra over a field is étale, the composite is étale.
For any étale subalgebra \(A \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\), base change to the separable closure satisfies: \[
A \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X) \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} = \mathcal{O}(X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}).
\] Since \(A \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} \cong \prod_{i=1}^m k^{\mathrm{sep}}\), it admits a complete system of orthogonal idempotents \(e_1, \dots, e_m\). Each \(e_i\) defines a non-empty open and closed subscheme \(V(1 - e_i)\) of \(X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}\). Thus \(m \le \#\{\text{connected components of } X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}\}\).
Because \(X\) is of finite type, it has finitely many connected components. The dimension \(\dim_k A\) is uniformly bounded, guaranteeing the existence of a unique maximal étale subalgebra.



Definition 2 (The Scheme \(\pi_0(X)\))  

Let \(A \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\) be the largest étale \(k\)-subalgebra. We define: \[
\pi_0(X) := \operatorname{Spec} A.
\] The inclusion \(A \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}(X)\) induces a canonical morphism \(X \to \pi_0(X)\).
Universal Property: For any étale \(k\)-scheme \(Y\) and any \(k\)-morphism \(f: X \to Y\), there exists a unique morphism \(\bar{f}: \pi_0(X) \to Y\) such that the following diagram commutes: \[
\begin{CD}
X @>{f}>> Y \\
@VVV @| \\
\pi_0(X) @>{\exists! \bar{f}}>> Y
\end{CD}
\]
Properties:

The fibers of \(X \to \pi_0(X)\) are the connected components of \(X\).
For every \(y \in \pi_0(X)\), the fiber \(X_y\) is geometrically connected over the residue field \(k(y)\).
\(\pi_0\) preserves finite products: \(\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \pi_0(X) \times_k \pi_0(Y)\).
The canonical morphism \(X \to \pi_0(X)\) is fppf.




Proposition 7 (Geometric Connectedness Criteria)  

If \(X\) is connected and \(X(k) \neq \emptyset\), then \(X\) is geometrically connected.
If \(X\) is geometrically connected and \(Y\) is connected, then \(X \times_k Y\) is connected.



Proof. 

If \(X\) is connected, \(\pi_0(X) = \operatorname{Spec} L\), where \(L/k\) is a finite separable field extension. A rational point \(x \in X(k)\) provides a section \(\operatorname{Spec} k \to X \to \operatorname{Spec} L\), forcing \(L \cong k\). Thus \(\pi_0(X) = \operatorname{Spec} k\), so \(X\) is geometrically connected.
We have \(\pi_0(X) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k\). By product preservation, \[
\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \pi_0(X) \times_k \pi_0(Y) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k \times_k \pi_0(Y) \cong \pi_0(Y).
\] Since \(Y\) is connected, \(\pi_0(Y) = \operatorname{Spec} L\) for a field \(L\). Thus \(\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \operatorname{Spec} L\), which shows \(X \times_k Y\) is connected.



Definition 3 (The Identity Component \(G^\circ\))  

The identity component \(G^\circ\) of an algebraic group \(G\) is the connected component containing the identity section \(e\). Endowed with its open subscheme structure, \(G^\circ\) is a smooth, geometrically connected, open and closed normal subgroup scheme of \(G\).
For any open subgroup \(G' \subseteq G\) of finite index, \(G^\circ \subseteq G' \subseteq G\), and \((G^\circ)^\circ = G^\circ\).



Proposition 8 (\(\pi_0(G)\) and the Connected Component) Let \(G\) be an algebraic group over \(k\).

\(\pi_0(G)\) is a finite étale group scheme over \(k\), and the canonical morphism \(G \to \pi_0(G)\) is a homomorphism of algebraic groups.
The identity component \(G^\circ := \ker(G \to \pi_0(G))\) is a geometrically connected, normal closed and open subgroup scheme of \(G\). For any field extension \(L/k\), we have \((G_L)^\circ = (G^\circ)_L\).
\(G\) is connected \(\iff \pi_0(G) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k \iff G\) is geometrically connected.
Formation of the identity component commutes with products: \((G \times_k H)^\circ \cong G^\circ \times_k H^\circ\).
If \(H\) is a connected group scheme over \(k\), any homomorphism \(\psi: H \to G\) factors uniquely through \(G^\circ \hookrightarrow G\).



Proof. 

Since \(\pi_0\) commutes with finite products, the group morphisms \(m, i, e\) on \(G\) induce group structure morphisms on \(\pi_0(G)\) by functoriality.
For (3), since \(e \in G^\circ(k)\), \(G^\circ\) has a \(k\)-rational point. Proposition 7(1) implies that \(G^\circ\) is geometrically connected.
For (5), since \(H\) is connected, \(\pi_0(H) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k\). Functoriality yields a commutative diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
H @>{\psi}>> G \\
@VVV @VVV \\
\pi_0(H) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k @>{e}>> \pi_0(G)
\end{CD}
\] Thus the composition \(H \to G \to \pi_0(G)\) is the trivial map, which implies that \(\psi\) factors uniquely through \(G^\circ = \ker(G \to \pi_0(G))\).



Definition 4 (Exact Sequences of Group Schemes) A sequence of homomorphisms of group schemes over \(k\): \[
1 \longrightarrow N \xrightarrow{\quad i \quad} G \xrightarrow{\quad p \quad} Q \longrightarrow 1
\] is said to be exact if:

\(i: N \hookrightarrow G\) is a closed immersion identifying \(N\) with a normal subgroup scheme of \(G\);
\(p: G \to Q\) is an fppf morphism;
\(i(N) = \ker(p)\).

title: 22.0 Preliminaries
text:
Definition 1 (Cartier Divisor) Let \(X\) be an irreducible complex variety. Let \(\mathcal{M}_X := \mathcal{K}_X\) be the constant sheaf of rational functions on \(X\), and \(\mathcal{O}_X \subseteq \mathcal{M}_X\) the structure sheaf.

A Cartier divisor on \(X\) is a global section of the quotient sheaf of units \(\mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*\). The abelian group of Cartier divisors on \(X\) is denoted by: \[
\operatorname{Div}(X) := \Gamma(X, \mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*).
\]
In terms of local data, a Cartier divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) is represented by a collection of pairs \(\{(U_i, f_i)\}_{i \in I}\), where \(\{U_i\}\) is an open covering of \(X\), \(f_i \in \Gamma(U_i, \mathcal{M}_X^*)\), and on overlaps \(U_{ij} = U_i \cap U_j\), \[
\frac{f_i}{f_j} = g_{ij} \in \Gamma(U_{ij}, \mathcal{O}_X^*).
\] Two such collections \(\{(U_i, f_i)\}\) and \(\{(V_j, g_j)\}\) determine the same Cartier divisor if they agree on a common refinement \(\{W_k\}\), that is, \(f_k / g_k \in \Gamma(W_k, \mathcal{O}_X^*)\).
The support of \(D\) is the closed subset: \[
\operatorname{Supp}(D) := \big\{ x \in X \;\big|\; (f_i)_x \notin \mathcal{O}_{X, x}^* \text{ for } x \in U_i \big\}.
\]
The group operation is written additively: for \(D = \{(U_i, f_i)\}\) and \(D' = \{(U_i, f_i')\}\), \[
D + D' = \{(U_i, f_i f_i')\}.
\]
A Cartier divisor \(D\) is effective (denoted \(D \ge 0\)) if it can be represented by local equations \(f_i \in \Gamma(U_i, \mathcal{O}_X)\) for all \(i\). We write \(D \ge D'\) if and only if \(D - D' \ge 0\).



Remark 1 (Sheaf of Meromorphic Functions on Non-Reduced Schemes). If \(X\) is not necessarily reduced, \(\mathcal{M}_X\) is defined as the sheaf of total quotient rings: for an affine open \(U = \operatorname{Spec} A\), \[
\mathcal{M}_X(U) := A_{\mathrm{tot}},
\] where \(A_{\mathrm{tot}} = S^{-1}A\) is the localization of \(A\) at the multiplicatively closed set \(S \subseteq A\) of all non-zero-divisors. Then \(\mathcal{O}_X^* \subseteq \mathcal{M}_X^*\), and Cartier divisors are defined identically.


Definition 2 (Cycles and Weil Divisors)  

Let \(X\) be a variety (or scheme) of pure dimension \(n\). A \(k\)-cycle on \(X\) is a formal \(\mathbb{Z}\)-linear combination of \(k\)-dimensional irreducible subvarieties of \(X\). The abelian group of \(k\)-cycles is denoted by \(Z_k(X)\).
A Weil divisor on \(X\) is an \((n-1)\)-cycle, so the group of Weil divisors is \(\operatorname{WDiv}(X) := Z_{n-1}(X)\).
If \(X\) is irreducible, for any \(f \in \mathcal{K}(X)^*\) and any prime divisor \(V \in Z_{n-1}(X)\), we define: \[
\operatorname{ord}_V(f) := \operatorname{ord}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{X, V}}(f),
\] where \(\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{X, V}\) is the normalization of the local ring \(\mathcal{O}_{X, V}\) in \(\mathcal{K}(X)\). The rational function \(f\) defines a principal Weil divisor: \[
\operatorname{div}(f) = \sum_{V \subseteq X} \operatorname{ord}_V(f) [V].
\]



Proposition 1 (Cycle Map) There is a canonical cycle homomorphism: \[
\operatorname{cyc}: \operatorname{Div}(X) \longrightarrow \operatorname{WDiv}(X), \quad D \longmapsto [D] := \sum_{V \subseteq X} \operatorname{ord}_V(D) \cdot [V],
\] where \(\operatorname{ord}_V(D) = \operatorname{ord}_V(f_i)\) whenever the generic point \(\eta_V \in U_i\).

The map \(\operatorname{cyc}\) is injective if \(X\) is normal.
The map \(\operatorname{cyc}\) is an isomorphism if \(X\) is non-singular (regular).



Definition 3 (Principal Divisors and Rational Sections)  

For any global section \(f \in \Gamma(X, \mathcal{M}_X^*)\), \(f\) defines a principal Cartier divisor: \[
\operatorname{div}(f) \in \Gamma(X, \mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*) = \operatorname{Div}(X).
\] The subgroup of principal divisors is denoted by \(\operatorname{PDiv}(X) \subseteq \operatorname{Div}(X)\).
Two Cartier divisors \(D_1, D_2\) are linearly equivalent (denoted \(D_1 \sim D_2\) or \(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{lin}} D_2\)) if: \[
D_1 - D_2 \in \operatorname{PDiv}(X).
\]
Let \(L\) be a line bundle on \(X\). For any global section \(s \in \Gamma(X, L)\), choosing local trivializations \(\psi_i: L|_{U_i} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{O}_{U_i}\) defines an effective Cartier divisor \(\{ (U_i, \psi_i(s)) \} \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\), denoted \(\operatorname{div}(s)_0\).
More generally, any non-zero rational section \(s \in \Gamma(X, L \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{M}_X)\) determines a Cartier divisor \(\operatorname{div}(s) \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\).



Definition 4 (The Sheaf \(\mathcal{O}_X(D)\))  

Every Cartier divisor \(D = \{(U_i, f_i)\} \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) determines an invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{O}_X(D)\) (or \(\mathcal{L}(D)\)) whose local sections are: \[
\mathcal{O}_X(D)(U) := \big\{ s \in \Gamma(U, \mathcal{M}_X) \;\big|\; \operatorname{div}(s)|_U + D|_U \ge 0 \big\}.
\] Locally on each open set \(U_i\), multiplication by \(f_i\) yields an isomorphism: \[
\mathcal{O}_X(D)(U_i) \xrightarrow{\quad \times f_i \quad} \mathcal{O}_X(U_i), \quad s \longmapsto f_i \cdot s,
\] since \(\operatorname{div}(f_i s) = \operatorname{div}(f_i) + \operatorname{div}(s) \ge 0 \implies f_i s \in \mathcal{O}_X(U_i)\).
From the short exact sequence of sheaves on \(X\): \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X^* \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}_X^* \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^* \longrightarrow 0,
\] the connecting homomorphism gives: \[
\delta: \operatorname{Div}(X) = \Gamma(X, \mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*) \longrightarrow H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X^*) = \operatorname{Pic}(X).
\] Furthermore, \(\mathcal{O}_X(D_1) \cong \mathcal{O}_X(D_2) \iff D_1 \sim D_2\).
This construction induces an isomorphism: \[
\operatorname{CaCl}(X) := \operatorname{Div}(X) / \operatorname{PDiv}(X) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Pic}(X)
\] whenever \(X\) is reduced or projective.



Definition 5 (Linear Series and Base Locus)  

Let \(X\) be a variety and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\). Let \(V \subseteq H^0(X, L)\) be a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace. The linear series associated with \(V\) is: \[
|V| := \mathbb{P}(V^*) = \mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{sub}}(V),
\] the projective space of 1-dimensional subspaces in \(V\). If \(H^0(X, L)\) is finite-dimensional, \(|H^0(X, L)|\) is denoted by \(|L|\) and called the complete linear series.
The evaluation homomorphism is given by: \[
\mathrm{eval}_V: V \otimes_k \mathcal{O}_X \longrightarrow L, \quad s \otimes f \longmapsto f \cdot s|_U.
\]
The base ideal \(\mathfrak{b}(|V|) \subseteq \mathcal{O}_X\) of \(|V|\) is the image of the dualized evaluation: \[
V \otimes_k L^\vee \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X, \quad s \otimes \phi \longmapsto \phi(s).
\] The base scheme is the closed subscheme \(\operatorname{Bs}(|V|) \subseteq X\) defined by \(\mathfrak{b}(|V|)\). For a divisor \(D\), we write \(\mathfrak{b}(|D|)\) and \(\operatorname{Bs}(|D|)\) for the base ideal and locus of \(|\mathcal{O}_X(D)|\).



Definition 6 (Base-Point-Free Linear Series)  

A linear series \(|V|\) is free (or base-point-free) if its base ideal is trivial: \(\mathfrak{b}(|V|) = \mathcal{O}_X\) (equivalently, \(\operatorname{Bs}(|V|) = \emptyset\)).
A divisor \(D\) or a line bundle \(L\) is free if its complete linear series is base-point-free.
A line bundle \(L\) is free if and only if \(L\) is generated by its global sections.



Proposition 2 (Maps to Projective Space)  

If \(\dim_k V \ge 1\) and \(B = \operatorname{Bs}(|V|)\), then \(|V|\) defines a morphism: \[
\phi_{|V|}: X \setminus B \longrightarrow \mathbb{P} V = \operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym} V).
\]
If \(W \subseteq V\) is a linear subspace, we have a commutative naturality diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
X \setminus \operatorname{Bs}(|V|) @>{\phi_{|V|}}>> \mathbb{P} V \setminus \mathbb{P}(V/W) \\
@VVV @VV{\pi}V \\
X \setminus \operatorname{Bs}(|W|) @>{\phi_{|W|}}>> \mathbb{P} W
\end{CD}
\] where \(\pi\) is the linear projection with center \(\mathbb{P}(V/W)\).



Definition 7 (Intersection Number (Snapper’s Formulation))  

Let \(X\) be a proper variety over \(k\). Let \(Y \hookrightarrow X\) be an irreducible subvariety of dimension \(m = \dim Y\). For any line bundles \(L_1, \dots, L_m \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\), the intersection number is defined by: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y) := \sum_{I \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\}} (-1)^{|I|} \chi\left(X, \bigotimes_{i \in I} L_i^\vee \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} i_* \mathcal{O}_Y\right) = \sum_{I \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\}} (-1)^{|I|} \chi\left(Y, \bigotimes_{i \in I} L_i^\vee|_Y\right).
\]
If \(Y = X\) with \(\dim X = n\), we write \((L_1 \cdots L_n)\) instead of \((L_1 \cdots L_n \cdot X)\). Then: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y) = (L_1|_Y \cdots L_m|_Y).
\]
For a general subscheme \(Y \subseteq X\) of pure dimension \(m\), associated with the cycle \([Y] = \sum_j \operatorname{length}_{\mathcal{O}_{Y, \eta_j}}(\mathcal{O}_{Y, \eta_j}) [Y_j]\), the intersection number is defined by linearity: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y) := \sum_j \operatorname{length}(\mathcal{O}_{Y, \eta_j}) (L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y_j).
\]
If \(L_i \cong \mathcal{O}_X(D_i)\), we also write \((D_1 \cdots D_m \cdot Y)\) for \((L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y)\).




Convention: From now on, unless otherwise stated, every scheme is assumed to be separated, proper, and of finite type over an algebraically closed field \(k = \bar{k}\) with \(\operatorname{char}(k) = 0\). A variety is defined as an irreducible and reduced scheme.



Proposition 3 (Basic Properties of Intersection Numbers)  

Let \(X\) be a proper curve and \(L \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\). Then \((L \cdot X) = \deg L\). If \(X\) is a proper variety and \(C \subseteq X\) is a curve, \((L \cdot C) = \deg(L|_C)\).
Let \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) be an effective Cartier divisor. If \(Y \subseteq X\) is an irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n = \dim Y\) such that \(D\) intersects \(Y\) properly (\(Y \not\subseteq \operatorname{Supp} D\)), then \(D|_Y\) is of pure dimension \(n - 1\) and: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_{n-1} \cdot \mathcal{O}_X(D) \cdot Y) = (L_1 \cdots L_{n-1} \cdot D|_Y).
\]
The intersection product is \(\mathbb{Z}\)-multilinear and symmetric: \[
\operatorname{Pic}(X)^m \times A_m(X) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}, \quad (L_1, \dots, L_m, [Y]) \longmapsto (L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot [Y]).
\] In particular, if \(Y_1 \sim_{\mathrm{rat}} Y_2\) are rationally equivalent cycles, then: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y_1) = (L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y_2).
\]



Definition 8 (Numerical Equivalence)  

Two line bundles \(L_1, L_2 \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) are numerically equivalent (denoted \(L_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} L_2\)) if for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\), \[
(L_1 \cdot C) = (L_2 \cdot C).
\] Two Cartier divisors \(D_1, D_2\) are numerically equivalent (denoted \(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} D_2\)) if \(\mathcal{O}_X(D_1) \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} \mathcal{O}_X(D_2)\).
The quotient group: \[
N^1(X) := \operatorname{Pic}(X) / \equiv_{\mathrm{num}}
\] is called the Néron-Severi group of \(X\) (modulo numerical equivalence).



Proposition 4 (The Néron-Severi Group and Picard Number)  

\(N^1(X)\) is torsion-free.
\(N^1(X)\) is a finitely generated free abelian group.
The rank \(\rho(X) := \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Z}} N^1(X)\) is called the Picard number of \(X\).



Lemma 1 (Numerical Invariance of Intersection) If \(L_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} L_1', \dots, L_k \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} L_k'\), then for any subvariety \(V \subseteq X\) of pure dimension \(k\), \[
(L_1 \cdots L_k \cdot [V]) = (L_1' \cdots L_k' \cdot [V]).
\]


Theorem 1 (Asymptotic Riemann-Roch I)  

Let \(X\) be an irreducible proper variety of dimension \(n = \dim X\), and \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\). As \(m \to \infty\), \[
\chi(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\] More generally, for any coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), \[
\chi(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{F}) \cdot \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\]
If \(D\) is ample, then by Serre vanishing \(H^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = 0\) for all \(i > 0\) and \(m \gg 0\), hence: \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}),
\] and for any \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{F}) \cdot \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\]



Proposition 5 (Amplitude Checked on Curves and Reduction)  

Let \(f: Y \to X\) be a finite morphism of proper schemes. If \(L \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) is ample, then \(f^* L \in \operatorname{Pic}(Y)\) is ample.
A line bundle \(L \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) is ample if and only if \(L|_{X_{\mathrm{red}}}\) is ample, if and only if \(L|_{X_{i, \mathrm{red}}}\) is ample for every irreducible component \(X_i\) of \(X\).
Let \(L\) be a globally generated line bundle on a proper scheme \(X\). Then \(L\) is ample if and only if \((L \cdot C) > 0\) for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\).



Proof. Proof of (3). Consider the following three assertions: - (a) \(L\) is ample; - (b) The morphism \(\phi = \phi_{|L|}: X \to \mathbb{P} H^0(X, L)\) is finite; - (c) \((L \cdot C) > 0\) for all irreducible curves \(C \subseteq X\).
We show \((b) \implies (a) \implies (c) \implies (b)\):

\((b) \implies (a)\): Since \(\phi\) is finite and \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(1)\) is ample, \(L \cong \phi^* \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(1)\) is ample by (1).
\((a) \implies (c)\): If \(L\) is ample, its restriction to any curve \(C \subseteq X\) is ample, hence \((L \cdot C) = \deg(L|_C) > 0\).
\((c) \implies (b)\): Suppose \(\phi\) is not finite. Since \(\phi\) is a proper morphism, it cannot be quasi-finite. Hence there exists a point \(p \in \phi(X)\) such that \(\dim \phi^{-1}(p) \ge 1\). Choose an irreducible curve \(Z \subseteq \phi^{-1}(p) \subseteq X\). Endow \(Z\) with the reduced structure.
The restriction \(\phi|_Z: Z \to \mathbb{P}^N\) has set-theoretic image \(\{p\}\). Because \(Z\) is reduced, the scheme-theoretic image \(\operatorname{Im}(\phi|_Z)\) is reduced, meaning \(\operatorname{Im}(\phi|_Z) = \operatorname{Spec} k(p) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^N\). Thus the pullback bundle: \[
L|_Z = (\phi|_Z)^* \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N}(1) \cong \mathcal{O}_Z
\] is trivial. Consequently, \((L \cdot Z) = \deg(\mathcal{O}_Z) = 0\), contradicting assumption (c). Thus \(\phi\) is finite, completing the proof.



Proposition 6 (Asymptotic Riemann-Roch II) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) be an ample Cartier divisor. Then: \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\] For any coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{F}) \cdot \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\]


Proposition 7 (Intersection with Complete Intersections in \(\mathbb{P}^N\)) Let \(X = \mathbb{P}^N\), and let \(Y \subseteq X\) be an irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n\). If \(H_1, \dots, H_n\) are effective hypersurfaces of degrees \(d_1, \dots, d_n\) in \(\mathbb{P}^N\), then: \[
(\mathcal{O}_X(H_1) \cdots \mathcal{O}_X(H_n) \cdot Y) = d_1 \cdots d_n \deg(Y).
\]


Proposition 8 (Projection Formula for Intersections) Let \(\pi: X_1 \to X_2\) be a morphism of integral proper schemes of the same dimension \(n\). For any line bundles \(L_1, \dots, L_n \in \operatorname{Pic}(X_2)\), \[
(\pi^* L_1 \cdots \pi^* L_n) = \deg(X_1 / X_2) \cdot (L_1 \cdots L_n).
\]


Theorem 2 (Cartier Class Group and Picard Group) If \(X\) is a reduced Noetherian scheme, then: \[
\operatorname{CaCl}(X) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Pic}(X).
\]


Proof. Proof idea. We show that \(H^1(X, \mathcal{K}_X^*) = 0\). Let \(X = \bigcup_{j=1}^m \overline{\{\eta_j\}}\) be the decomposition into irreducible components with generic points \(\eta_j\). Then: \[
\mathcal{K}_X^* = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m (i_{\eta_j})_* K_j^*,
\] which is a direct sum of pushforwards of constant sheaves from points, hence \(\mathcal{K}_X^*\) is flasque. Therefore \(H^1(X, \mathcal{K}_X^*) = 0\). Taking cohomology of the short exact sequence \(0 \to \mathcal{O}_X^* \to \mathcal{K}_X^* \to \mathcal{K}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^* \to 0\) yields: \[
H^0(X, \mathcal{K}_X^*) \xrightarrow{\;\operatorname{div}\;} H^0(X, \mathcal{K}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*) \longrightarrow H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X^*) \longrightarrow 0,
\] which implies: \[
\operatorname{coker}(\operatorname{div}) = \operatorname{Div}(X) / \operatorname{PDiv}(X) = \operatorname{CaCl}(X) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Pic}(X).
\]


Theorem 3 (Cartier Divisors vs. Weil Divisors) Let \(X\) be an irreducible variety that is regular in codimension 1. Then the cycle map induces injective homomorphisms: \[
\operatorname{Div}(X) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{WDiv}(X) \quad \text{and} \quad \operatorname{CaCl}(X) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Cl}(X).
\] In particular, if \(X\) is smooth (or regular), these maps are isomorphisms.

title: 22.3 Iitaka Fibration
text:
Definition 1 (Semigroup of a Line Bundle and Exponent) Let \(X\) be a variety and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\).

The set: \[
N(L) = N(X, L) := \big\{ m \ge 0 \;\big|\; H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \neq 0 \big\}
\] forms a sub-semigroup of \((\mathbb{N}, +)\).
If \(N(L) \neq \{0\}\), there exists a unique integer \(e = e(L) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\) such that: \[
N(L) \subseteq e \mathbb{N} \quad \text{and} \quad e\mathbb{N} \setminus N(L) \text{ is finite}.
\] The integer \(e(L)\) is called the exponent of \(L\).



Proposition 1 (Scheme-Theoretic Image of a Rational Map) Let \(f: X \dashrightarrow Y\) be a rational map between irreducible varieties. For any representative morphism \((U, f_U)\) of \(f\) defined on a dense open set \(U \subseteq X\), the closed subvariety: \[
\operatorname{Im}(f) := \overline{f_U(U)} \subseteq Y
\] is independent of the chosen representative and is called the image of \(f\).


Proof. If \((V, f_V)\) is another representative, then \(f_U|_{U \cap V} = f_V|_{U \cap V}\). Setting \(W = U \cap V\), the pullback \(\mathcal{O}_Y \to (f_U)_* \mathcal{O}_U \to (f_W)_* \mathcal{O}_W\) has the same kernel because \(W\) is dense in \(U\) and \(X\) is reduced. The kernel defines the vanishing ideal of the scheme-theoretic closure, so \(\overline{f_U(U)} = \overline{f_W(W)} = \overline{f_V(V)}\).


Definition 2 (Iitaka Dimension) Let \(X\) be a normal variety and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\).

For each \(m \in N(X, L)\), the complete linear system \(|L^{\otimes m}|\) determines a rational map: \[
\phi_m := \phi_{|L^{\otimes m}|}: X \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P} H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}).
\]
The Iitaka dimension (or \(L\)-dimension) of \(L\) is defined by: \[
\kappa(L) = \kappa(X, L) := \begin{cases} \max_{m \in N(X, L)} \big\{ \dim \operatorname{Im}(\phi_m) \big\}, & N(X, L) \neq \{0\}, \\ -\infty, & N(X, L) = \{0\}. \end{cases}
\]
For an arbitrary non-normal variety \(X\), let \(\nu: \widetilde{X} \to X\) be the normalization. The Iitaka dimension is defined by: \[
\kappa(X, L) := \kappa(\widetilde{X}, \nu^* L).
\]



Definition 3 (Algebraic Fiber Space) An algebraic fiber space (AFS) is a surjective projective morphism \(f: X \to Y\) between irreducible varieties such that: \[
f_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Y.
\] By Zariski’s Connectedness Principle, every fiber of an algebraic fiber space is connected.



Convention: From now on, \(X\) is assumed to be an irreducible normal projective variety over \(k\).



Proposition 2 (Powers Achieving the Iitaka Dimension) Let \(X\) be a normal variety and \(\kappa = \kappa(X, L) \ge 0\). Then: \[
\dim \operatorname{Im}(\phi_m) = \kappa \quad \text{for all } m \gg 0 \text{ with } m \in N(X, L).
\]


Proof. Replacing \(L\) by \(L^{\otimes e(L)}\), we may assume \(e(L) = 1\). Then there exists \(p_0\) such that \(H^0(X, L^{\otimes p}) \neq 0\) for all \(p \ge p_0\). Fix a non-zero section \(s \in H^0(X, L^{\otimes p})\).
Choose \(m\) such that \(\dim \operatorname{Im}(\phi_m) = \kappa\). Multiplication by \(s\) induces an injection \(H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \hookrightarrow H^0(X, L^{\otimes(m+p)})\). This linear inclusion determines a rational projection of projective spaces: \[
\begin{CD}
X @>{\phi_{m+p}}>> Y_{m+p} \\
@| @VV{\pi}V \\
X @>{\phi_m}>> Y_m
\end{CD}
\] Because \(\pi\) is a dominant rational projection, we have: \[
\kappa = \dim Y_m \le \dim Y_{m+p} \le \kappa \implies \dim Y_{m+p} = \kappa.
\] Thus \(\dim \operatorname{Im}(\phi_n) = \kappa\) for all \(n \ge m + p_0\).


Proposition 3 (Criterion for Algebraic Fiber Spaces) Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a surjective projective morphism between normal varieties, inducing an inclusion of function fields \(K(Y) \subseteq K(X)\). Then \(f\) is an algebraic fiber space if and only if \(K(Y)\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X)\).
In particular, every projective surjective birational morphism between normal varieties is an algebraic fiber space.


Proof. \((\implies)\): Let \(K(Y) \subseteq \mathbb{L} \subseteq K(X)\) be the algebraic closure of \(K(Y)\) in \(K(X)\). Normalizing \(Y\) in \(\mathbb{L}\) produces a factorization: \[
X \xrightarrow{\quad h \quad} Z \xrightarrow{\quad g \quad} Y,
\] where \(g: Z \to Y\) is finite and \(h\) is proper. Since \(f\) is surjective and projective, \(h(X) = Z\), so \(\dim Z = \dim Y\). The condition \(f_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Y\) implies: \[
\mathcal{O}_Y \subseteq g_* \mathcal{O}_Z \subseteq g_* h_* \mathcal{O}_X = f_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Y \implies g_* \mathcal{O}_Z = \mathcal{O}_Y.
\] Since \(Y\) is normal, \(g\) must be an isomorphism, so \(\mathbb{L} = K(Y)\).
\((\impliedby)\): Consider the Stein factorization of \(f\): \[
X \xrightarrow{\quad \phi \quad} Z \xrightarrow{\quad g \quad} Y,
\] where \(\phi_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Z\) and \(g\) is finite. Since \(X\) is normal and \(\phi_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Z\), the scheme \(Z\) is normal. Furthermore, \(K(Z) \subseteq K(X)\) is a finite algebraic extension of \(K(Y)\). Since \(K(Y)\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X)\), we must have \(K(Z) = K(Y)\). Because \(Y\) is normal and \(g\) is birational and finite, Zariski’s Main Theorem implies that \(g: Z \xrightarrow{\sim} Y\) is an isomorphism. Thus \(f_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Y\).


Lemma 1 (Invariance of Sections and Picard Group) Let \(\phi: X \to Y\) be an algebraic fiber space.

For every line bundle \(L\) on \(Y\), the natural map is an isomorphism: \[
H^0(Y, L) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} H^0(X, \phi^* L).
\]
The pullback homomorphism \(\phi^*: \operatorname{Pic}(Y) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) is injective.



Proof. 

By the projection formula, \(\phi_* \phi^* L \cong L \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_Y} \phi_* \mathcal{O}_X \cong L\). Taking global sections yields \(H^0(X, \phi^* L) \cong H^0(Y, \phi_* \phi^* L) \cong H^0(Y, L)\).
If \(\phi^* L \cong \mathcal{O}_X\), then by (1), \(H^0(Y, L) \cong H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X) \cong k\) and \(H^0(Y, L^\vee) \cong H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X) \cong k\). Choose non-zero sections \(s \in H^0(Y, L)\) and \(t \in H^0(Y, L^\vee)\). The product \(s \otimes t \in H^0(Y, \mathcal{O}_Y) \cong k\) is non-zero, hence a non-zero constant \(c \in k^\times\). Thus \(s\) vanishes nowhere, which implies \(L \cong \mathcal{O}_Y\).



Definition 4 (Stable Base Locus) Let \(D\) be a Cartier divisor on \(X\).

The stable base locus of \(D\) is the closed set: \[
\mathbf{B}(D) := \bigcap_{m \ge 1} \operatorname{Bs}(|mD|).
\]
Since the family of closed sets satisfies \(\operatorname{Bs}(|m_1 D|) \cap \operatorname{Bs}(|m_2 D|) \supseteq \operatorname{Bs}(|(m_1 + m_2)D|)\), by the descending chain condition on closed subsets of \(X\), there exists \(m_0 \ge 1\) such that: \[
\mathbf{B}(D) = \operatorname{Bs}(|k m_0 D|) \quad \text{for all } k \gg 0.
\]



Definition 5 (Semiample Line Bundles)  

Define the semigroup of free multiples: \[
M(X, L) := \big\{ m \in \mathbb{N} \;\big|\; L^{\otimes m} \text{ is base-point-free} \big\}.
\] Let \(f = f(L)\) be the exponent of the semigroup \(M(X, L)\).
A line bundle \(L\) on \(X\) is semiample if \(M(X, L) \neq \{0\}\), that is, some positive power \(L^{\otimes m}\) is generated by its global sections.



Theorem 1 (Semiample Fibration) Let \(X\) be a normal projective variety and \(L\) a semiample line bundle on \(X\). Then there exists an algebraic fiber space \(\phi: X \to Y\) and an ample line bundle \(A\) on \(Y\) such that:

For all \(m \in M(X, L)\) sufficiently large, the morphism \(\phi_m: X \to \mathbb{P} H^0(X, L^{\otimes m})\) has image \(Y_m \cong Y\), and factors through \(\phi\).
\(\phi^* A \cong L^{\otimes f(L)}\), and for \(k \gg 0\), the very ample embeddings \(\iota_{A^{\otimes k}}: Y \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P} H^0(Y, A^{\otimes k})\) make the following diagram commute: \[
\begin{CD}
X @>{\phi}>> Y \\
@| @VV{\cong}V \\
X @>{\phi_{kf}}>> Y_{kf}
\end{CD}
\] In particular, the target variety \(Y\) is normal and projective.



Definition 6 (Big Line Bundles and Divisors) A line bundle \(L\) on an irreducible projective variety \(X\) is big if: \[
\kappa(X, L) = \dim X.
\] A Cartier divisor \(D\) is big if \(\mathcal{O}_X(D)\) is big.


Theorem 2 (The Iitaka Fibration Theorem) Let \(X\) be a normal projective variety and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\) with \(\kappa(X, L) > 0\). Then there exists an algebraic fiber space between normal varieties: \[
\phi_\infty: X_\infty \longrightarrow Y_\infty,
\] unique up to birational equivalence, and a birational morphism \(u_\infty: X_\infty \to X\), such that for all \(k \in N(X, L)\) sufficiently large, there exists a birational map \(v_k: Y_\infty \dashrightarrow Y_k\) making the following diagram commute: \[
\begin{CD}
X_\infty @>{u_\infty}>> X \\
@V{\phi_\infty}VV @VV{\phi_k}V \\
Y_\infty @>{v_k}>{\approx}> Y_k
\end{CD}
\] where \(Y_k := \operatorname{Im}(\phi_k) \subseteq \mathbb{P} H^0(X, L^{\otimes k})\).


Proof. Replacing \(L\) by \(L^{\otimes e(L)}\), we may assume without loss of generality that \(e(L) = 1\).
Step 1: The stable fibration for a sub-semigroup \(m\mathbb{N}\). Fix \(m \in N(X, L)\) such that \(\dim Y_m = \kappa(X, L)\). Let \(\mathfrak{b} = \mathfrak{b}(|L^{\otimes m}|) \subseteq \mathcal{O}_X\) be the base ideal. Blow up \(\mathfrak{b}\) and normalize to obtain a projective birational morphism: \[
u_m: X_{(m)} := \operatorname{Bl}_{\mathfrak{b}}(X)^\nu \longrightarrow X.
\] Let \(E_m\) be the exceptional divisor on the blow-up, and \(F_m\) its pullback to \(X_{(m)}\). Define: \[
M_m := u_m^* L^{\otimes m} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_{(m)}}} \mathcal{O}_{X_{(m)}}(-F_m).
\] Because \(u_m: X_{(m)} \to X\) is a birational morphism between normal varieties, Proposition 3 implies that \(u_m\) is an algebraic fiber space. By Lemma 1, \(H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \cong H^0(X_{(m)}, u_m^* L^{\otimes m})\). Since all sections vanish along \(F_m\) by construction of the blow-up, restriction to \(F_m\) is zero, yielding an isomorphism: \[
H^0(X_{(m)}, M_m) \cong H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}).
\] Consequently, \(M_m\) is generated by its global sections and defines a morphism \(\phi_{M_m}: X_{(m)} \to \mathbb{P} H^0(X_{(m)}, M_m)\). By Theorem 1, the Stein factorization of \(\phi_{M_m^{\otimes k}}\) stabilizes for \(k \gg 0\) to an algebraic fiber space: \[
\phi_{(m)}: X_{(m)} \longrightarrow Y_{(m)}.
\] For every \(k \ge 1\), we have \(H^0(X_{(m)}, M_m^{\otimes k}) \subseteq H^0(X_{(m)}, u_m^* L^{\otimes mk})\), inducing a dominant rational projection \(\mu_k: Y_{mk} \dashrightarrow Y_{(m)}\). Since \(X_{(m)} \to Y_{(m)}\) is an AFS, \(K(Y_{(m)})\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X_{(m)})\). The extension \(K(Y_{mk})/K(Y_{(m)})\) is algebraic and contained in \(K(X_{(m)})\), forcing: \[
K(Y_{mk}) = K(Y_{(m)}).
\] Hence \(\mu_k: Y_{mk} \dashrightarrow Y_{(m)}\) is birational for all \(k \gg 0\).
Step 2: Construction of \(X_\infty\) and \(Y_\infty\). Choose two coprime integers \(p, q \in N(X, L)\) such that \(\dim Y_p = \dim Y_q = \kappa(X, L)\) (which is possible since \(H^0(X, L) \neq 0\)). Apply Step 1 to \(M_p\) and \(M_q\), obtaining: \[
\phi_{(p)}: X_{(p)} \longrightarrow Y_{(p)}, \qquad \phi_{(q)}: X_{(q)} \longrightarrow Y_{(q)}.
\] Let \(\widetilde{U}\) be the closure of the diagonal embedding of a common dense open set \(U \subseteq X\) into \(X_{(p)} \times_X X_{(q)}\). Let \(X_\infty\) be the normalization of \(\widetilde{U}\). The projection maps \(v_p: X_\infty \to X_{(p)}\) and \(v_q: X_\infty \to X_{(q)}\) are projective, birational morphisms between normal varieties, hence algebraic fiber spaces.
Define the semiample line bundle: \[
M_{pq} := v_p^* M_p^{\otimes m_1} \otimes v_q^* M_q^{\otimes m_2}.
\] The morphism induced by \(|M_{pq}|\) factors as: \[
X_\infty \longrightarrow Y_\infty \xrightarrow{\quad w \quad} Y_{(p)} \times Y_{(q)},
\] where \(w\) is a finite morphism onto its image. Thus \(K(Y_\infty) = K(Y_{(p)}) = K(Y_{(q)})\), and \(K(Y_\infty)\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X_\infty)\). Hence \(\phi_\infty: X_\infty \to Y_\infty\) is an algebraic fiber space with \(\dim Y_\infty = \kappa(X, L)\).
For any \(k \gg 0\), the Frobenius coin problem ensures that \(k = c p^{m_1} + d q^{m_2}\) for integers \(c, d \ge 1\). The sheaf \(u_p^* M_p^{\otimes(c-1)p^{m_1}} \otimes u_q^* M_q^{\otimes(d-1)q^{m_2}}\) has a non-zero section, inducing an inclusion: \[
H^0(X_\infty, M_{pq}) \hookrightarrow H^0(X_\infty, u_\infty^* L^{\otimes k}).
\] This gives an induced dominant rational map \(v_k: Y_\infty \dashrightarrow Y_k\). Since \(\dim Y_k = \kappa(X, L) = \dim Y_\infty\) and \(K(Y_\infty)\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X_\infty)\), \(v_k\) is birational. Uniqueness follows because any two such targets are birational to \(Y_k\).


Corollary 1 (Iitaka Dimension of the Fibers) Let \(\phi_\infty: X_\infty \to Y_\infty\) be the Iitaka fibration associated with \(L\), and let \(L_\infty := u_\infty^* L\). For a very general closed point \(y \in Y_\infty\) (that is, \(y \in Y_\infty \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty F_i\) for countable proper closed subsets \(F_i \subsetneq Y_\infty\)), the fiber \(F := X_{\infty, y} = \phi_\infty^{-1}(y)\) satisfies: \[
\kappa(F, L_\infty|_F) = 0.
\]


Proof. By generic smoothness, a very general fiber \(F = X_{\infty, y}\) is smooth and connected (by Zariski’s Main Theorem), hence integral.
For all \(k \gg 0\), the rational map \(\phi_k \circ u_\infty\) is defined along \(F\) and contracts \(F\) to a single point \(\phi_k(u_\infty(F)) = \{p_k\} \subseteq Y_k\). Thus the image of the restriction map: \[
\rho_k: H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes k}) \longrightarrow H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F)
\] has dimension \(\le 1\) for all \(k \ge 1\).
Claim: Fix a very ample line bundle \(B\) on \(Y_\infty\). 1. There exists \(m_0 > 0\) such that \(H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes m_0} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^\vee) \neq 0\). 2. For any fixed \(k\) and all \(r \gg 0\), the restriction: \[
   \beta_{k, r}: H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^{\otimes r}) \longrightarrow H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^{\otimes r}|_F) \cong H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F)
   \] is surjective.
Proof of Claim: For (1), by the proof of Theorem 2, there exists an ample line bundle \(A\) on \(Y_\infty\) such that \(\phi_\infty^* A \subseteq L_\infty^{\otimes m_0}\). Because \(A\) is ample, \(A^{\otimes m_0} \otimes B^\vee\) has a non-zero section for \(m_0 \gg 0\), yielding a non-zero section \(s \in H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes m_0} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^\vee)\). For a very general fiber \(F\), \(s|_F \neq 0\).
For (2), by generic flatness, \(X_\infty \to Y_\infty\) is flat over a neighborhood of the generic point. By Grauert’s Semicontinuity Theorem, \((\phi_\infty)_* L_\infty^{\otimes k}\) is locally free near \(y\), and the fiber cohomology satisfies: \[
H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F) \cong (\phi_\infty)_* L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes k(y).
\] Since \(B\) is very ample on \(Y_\infty\), the sheaf \((\phi_\infty)_* L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes B^{\otimes r}\) is generated by its global sections for \(r \gg 0\). Hence the evaluation map \(\beta_{k, r}\) is surjective.
Now, for any \(r \ge 1\), multiplication by \(s^{\otimes r}\) yields an injection: \[
H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^{\otimes r}) \xrightarrow{\quad \times s^{\otimes r} \quad} H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes(k + r m_0)}).
\] Restricting to the fiber \(F\), we obtain a commutative diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^{\otimes r}) @>>> H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes(k + r m_0)}) \\
@VV{\beta_{k, r}}V @VV{\rho_{k + r m_0}}V \\
H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F) @>{\times (s|_F)^{\otimes r}}>> H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes(k + r m_0)}|_F)
\end{CD}
\] Because \(F\) is integral and \(s|_F \neq 0\), the bottom map is injective. Since \(\beta_{k, r}\) is surjective, the image of the bottom map is contained in \(\operatorname{Im}(\rho_{k + r m_0})\). However, \(\operatorname{rank}(\rho_{k + r m_0}) \le 1\), which forces: \[
h^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F) \le 1 \quad \text{for all } k \ge 1.
\] Since \(h^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F) = 1\) for all sufficiently large divisible \(k\), we conclude: \[
\kappa(F, L_\infty|_F) = 0.
\]
